mcqs.question: Using standard level-order BFS, how do you extract the right side view of a binary tree?
options: Take the first node processed at every level
Take the node with the largest value at every level
Take every node in the tree's rightmost subtree
Take the last node processed at every level, since that's the one visible when looking from the right
mcqs.explanation: Level-order BFS processes each level left to right, so the last node dequeued at a given level is the rightmost node at that depth — exactly what's visible looking from the right. Right view has nothing to do with value magnitude, and it isn't limited to the rightmost subtree, since a level's rightmost node can come from either side of the tree depending on shape.

mcqs.question: In the (row, column) coordinate scheme used for vertical-order and view problems, what happens to the column value on a right move versus a left move?
options: Column increases on a right move and decreases on a left move; row increases on both
Column stays the same regardless of direction; only row changes
Row increases on a right move only; column is unused
Column and row both increase on every move regardless of direction
mcqs.explanation: The whole point of the coordinate scheme is that column tracks horizontal position — incrementing on right moves, decrementing on left moves — while row simply tracks depth, increasing by one on every move regardless of direction. Column absolutely changes with direction (that's how columns are grouped at all), and row isn't restricted to only right moves.

mcqs.question: Why does using DFS discovery order (instead of BFS) for top-view tie-breaking risk producing the wrong answer?
options: DFS cannot assign column coordinates to nodes
DFS commits to one full path before exploring siblings, so it can visit a node from a deeper branch before a shallower node in another branch that should actually win the tie
DFS and BFS always produce identical discovery orders for any tree
Top view doesn't involve any ties in practice
mcqs.explanation: DFS's traversal order has no built-in relationship to depth across different branches — it can reach a deeper node in one column before a shallower, competing node in the same column simply because of path order, which breaks the 'shallowest wins' rule top view needs. Column assignment works fine under either traversal, DFS and BFS discovery orders genuinely differ, and same-column same-row ties are a real, common occurrence in view problems.

mcqs.question: What is the only real difference between computing top view and bottom view of a tree, once (row, column) coordinates are assigned?
options: Bottom view requires an entirely different coordinate system
Top view can only be computed with DFS; bottom view only with BFS
Bottom view doesn't support column grouping at all
Which node wins per column — top view keeps the smallest row, bottom view keeps the largest row — everything else about the coordinate assignment and grouping stays the same
mcqs.explanation: Both views reuse the identical coordinate scheme and the identical BFS discovery pass; only the per-column winner rule flips between 'keep the shallowest' and 'keep the deepest.' Both are typically implemented with BFS for correct tie-breaking, not restricted to different traversal types each, and bottom view uses the same column grouping as top view, not a different system.

mcqs.question: In diagonal traversal, what determines whether a child node shares its parent's diagonal group or starts a new one?
options: The child's row value, regardless of which side it's on
A right move keeps the same diagonal as the parent; a left move starts a new diagonal one greater than the parent's
Every child always starts a new diagonal, whether left or right
Diagonal grouping is identical to column-based vertical-order grouping
mcqs.explanation: Diagonal traversal's defining rule is that only left moves change the diagonal coordinate — a right child inherits the exact same diagonal as its parent, which is what makes an unbroken run of right children collapse into a single diagonal group. Row alone doesn't determine this, right children explicitly do not start a new diagonal, and this is a distinct coordinate scheme from vertical order's column-based grouping, which changes on both left and right moves.

mcqs.question: A top-view implementation tracks depth correctly via DFS recursion but relies on DFS visitation order alone to decide which of two same-column nodes was 'first.' What's wrong with this?
options: DFS visitation order has no guaranteed relationship to depth across different branches, so a deeper node can be visited before a shallower competing one, producing an incorrect topmost answer
Nothing — DFS recursion depth and DFS visitation order are always consistent with each other
This only fails when the tree has an even number of nodes
DFS cannot track depth at all, so this approach never compiles
mcqs.explanation: Tracking depth accurately doesn't fix the tie-breaking problem if the code still relies on visitation order to imply which node is shallower — DFS's traversal order and true depth ordering across branches aren't the same thing, and conflating them is exactly the bug described. This is unrelated to node count parity, DFS certainly can track depth via recursion, and the flaw is a logic issue, not a compilation one.
